items.desc: The malaria parasite is able to detect changes in its host's environment and respond by increasing the production of sexual forms capable of being transmitted to mosquitoes. A study led by the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal) identifies the molecular mechanism underlying this process. The findings, published in Nature Microbiology, answer what has been one of the major unanswered questions in malaria research for decades.

items.title: Sacred springs of South Africa—pure waters or polluted? We found tiny bits of plastic in the samples we tested
items.desc: Across South Africa, natural springs are more than sources of freshwater. Some are places of healing, spiritual cleansing and rituals, where communities collect water and maintain longstanding cultural connections with the environment. For example, during cleansing rituals, people bathe in or collect spring water as a way of seeking spiritual renewal, healing and protection. These are known as sacred springs.

items.title: Scientists opened a sealed envelope after 10 years. Gravity still didn’t make sense
items.desc: A decade-long NIST experiment has produced a new measurement of the universal gravitational constant that differs unexpectedly from another leading result, deepening a 225-year-old physics puzzle. The discrepancy is tiny, but for one of nature’s most fundamental constants, it is large enough to keep scientists wondering whether hidden experimental errors or something more surprising is involved.

items.title: A giant crater may reveal the origin of Mars’ doomed moon
items.desc: A massive crater on Mars’ moon Phobos may hide a dense region of compressed material that could reveal whether the moon is a captured asteroid or debris from an ancient impact on Mars. Japan’s upcoming MMX sample return mission could provide the measurements and physical evidence needed to solve the mystery.

items.title: Hurricane Hunters reveal 4 warning signs that a storm is about to strengthen
items.desc: Nearly three decades of Hurricane Hunter data reveal four features that can help a tilted tropical cyclone straighten its circulation and become capable of intensifying. The findings could give forecasters an earlier warning that a seemingly disorganized storm is becoming primed to strengthen.

items.title: Scientists may have solved a 2,000-year-old Dead Sea Scrolls mystery
items.desc: Researchers may have solved a long-running mystery surrounding the Dead Sea Scrolls by proposing that the Qumran sect really did use its distinctive 364-day calendar. Its perfectly ordered 52-week system kept holidays on the same weekdays, but it slowly drifted out of sync with the seasons because it was shorter than the true solar year.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden “ID card” in cat urine
items.desc: Cats may identify one another through a surprisingly durable chemical “calling card” made from 13 unusual fatty acids in their urine. The compounds appear linked to mysterious fat droplets in the kidneys and may represent a scent-recognition system shared across the cat family.

items.title: New nanoparticles make hidden chemical differences light up
items.desc: Scientists have developed ultra-bright nanoparticles that can detect tiny amounts of chemicals and distinguish between molecules that look almost identical. The technology could one day provide a cheaper way to catch dangerous drug impurities or trace pollutants using simple low-cost lasers.

items.title: Ancient DNA reveals how plague kept returning for 400 years after the Black Death
items.desc: Ancient DNA reveals that plague repeatedly returned to Europe for more than 400 years after the Black Death, evolving into new lineages and spreading through trade, migration, and war. Researchers also developed a method to date ancient plague genomes more precisely, linking many of them to specific outbreaks recorded in historical sources.

items.title: Einstein’s “spooky action” just survived one of physics’ most extreme tests
items.desc: Physicists have detected strong evidence that heavy, fleeting Z bosons can become quantum entangled during Higgs boson decays at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider. The result shows that Einstein’s “spooky action at a distance” survives even under some of the most extreme conditions ever created in a laboratory.

items.title: Scientists find that “perfect” systems may be surprisingly fragile
items.desc: Complex systems may work better when their parts are not perfectly alike. Northwestern physicists found that carefully balanced variation, or “disorder,” can make networks such as power grids, ecosystems, neurons, and materials more stable. Even random differences sometimes improved stability compared with completely uniform systems. The discovery could help researchers design more resilient technologies and explain why natural systems are so rarely perfectly uniform.

items.title: A 66-million-year-old tooth reveals T. rex was nearly as warm as a human
items.desc: Chemical clues preserved inside fossilized T. rex teeth reveal that the dinosaur maintained a body temperature of about 97 degrees Fahrenheit, almost identical to humans. The finding provides direct evidence that the giant predator was warm-blooded, helping explain how it stayed active and survived in chilly environments as far north as Alaska.

items.title: New chemical wipes out 95% of termites without harming humans
items.desc: A chemical that stops drywood termites from building new exoskeletons killed about 95% of colonies in testing, offering a potentially safer alternative to traditional fumigation. Because termites eventually have no choice but to molt, the treatment turns a normal stage of their life cycle into a fatal weakness.

items.title: Scientists solve a 50-year mystery and discover a new human blood group
items.desc: Scientists have identified the genetic cause behind the mysterious AnWj blood group antigen, solving a puzzle that began in 1972 and establishing a new blood group system called MAL. The discovery could make it much easier to find extremely rare AnWj-negative patients and donors and protect them from potentially dangerous transfusion reactions.

items.title: Scientists just named a new snake after Guns N’ Roses legend Slash
items.desc: A newly discovered snake from New Guinea has been named after Guns N’ Roses guitarist Slash, who has loved reptiles since childhood. Genetic testing and physical differences confirmed that the reddish-brown groundsnake, Lielaphis slashi, is a species scientists had never formally recognized before. The nonvenomous snake may use large rear teeth to catch slippery lizards and reptile eggs.

items.title: This tiny organism can shrink to one quarter its size in milliseconds
items.desc: A single-celled organism can shrink to one-quarter of its length in milliseconds using a remarkable calcium-powered protein “fishnet.” Scientists hope its unusual machinery could inspire artificial muscles capable of moving far faster than today’s designs.

items.title: This deep-sea enzyme survives heat that destroys most proteins
items.desc: A deep-sea microbe uses an exceptionally heat-resistant enzyme to turn atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia at temperatures that would destroy most proteins. Its unusual structure and a newly observed reaction state may reveal an ancient, shared mechanism behind nitrogen fixation and could eventually inspire cleaner biotechnology and fertilizer production.

items.title: Can Adaptation Accelerate Climate Action?
items.desc: After a summer of apocalyptic headlines, a new survey finds that people across the political spectrum are deeply concerned about preparing for the effects of global warming. The adaptation imperative may end up being the kind of crisis that forces us to stop neglecting the green agenda and act at the necessary scale.

items.title: Africa’s AI Opportunity
items.desc: The global AI revolution is often portrayed as a Sino-American race to develop the most advanced frontier models. But the greatest economic prize most likely will be found in deploying practical intelligence, particularly in Africa’s young, dynamic, and fast-growing economies.

items.title: The Political Earthquake From Germany’s China Shock
items.desc: For decades, Germany’s stability rested on an implicit bargain: high-value manufacturing would provide good jobs, strong export revenues, and broad-based prosperity, which political institutions would translate into social cohesion. Competition from China shakes that bargain to its foundations.

items.title: Stopping the Far Right’s Rise
items.desc: Leftists insist that what is behind the far right’s recent gains, from Europe to Central and South America, is economic precarity. Far-right leaders know better, winning elections or gaining support despite embracing very different economic policies.

items.title: Does Claude Have Rights?
items.desc: Given the many differences between brains and LLMs, claiming that an AI is or might be conscious requires a high bar of evidence. But Anthropic’s constitution for Claude brushes that caveat aside, suggesting that we attribute sentience to non-biological beings.

items.title: A Congress for Europe’s Future
items.desc: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's recently proposed Congress of Europe is a step in the right direction, given the scale of Europe's geopolitical challenges. But to succeed, it must address the shortcomings that have hampered similar efforts in the past.

items.title: Trump’s Iran Sanctions Have a China Problem
items.desc: US President Donald Trump is trying to pressure the Iranian regime by isolating it from the dollar-based financial system. But because Iran’s oil trade largely moves through Chinese banks and renminbi-based networks, those sanctions increasingly depend on financial institutions beyond American control.

items.title: When AI Stops Asking Permission
items.desc: The most useful lesson from this summer’s breach of Hugging Face by a swarm of OpenAI agents is about architecture, not intentions. AI agents need protective layers—limited access, separate authorization for sensitive actions, records nobody can quietly edit, and outside testing before deployment—not a lecture about good behavior.

items.title: Are Mexicans Really Better Off Under Claudia Sheinbaum?
items.desc: For two consecutive years, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has pointed to reductions in extreme poverty to argue that Mexicans are better off today than they were in 2018. But a more holistic look at the available socioeconomic data casts doubt on that rosy picture.

items.title: The UN’s Credibility Test
items.desc: Effective multilateralism depends on institutions that are transparent, accountable, and able to enforce their own rules. The United Nations should lead by example, from how it selects its next secretary-general to how it plans to ensure that governments follow through on their climate commitments.

items.title: A Workable Social Contract for the Climate Transition
items.desc: Economic insecurity and growing distrust in institutions are undermining governments’ ability to sustain support for climate action. To rebuild that support, they must show that climate policies can reduce household bills, create decent jobs, and ensure that the biggest emitters pay their fair share.

items.title: It’s Time to Reconsider Inflation Targeting
items.desc: Central banks were caught off guard by the inflationary surge of 2021–23 because they relied too heavily on inflation forecasts based on flawed models and ignored other warning signs. Their failure to recognize the rapid growth of the money supply, in particular, underscores the need to reassess their reliance on inflation targeting.

items.title: Democrats Need to Talk About Immigration
items.desc: Radical right-wing parties have advanced across Western countries by successfully tying immigration to voters’ diffuse fears about their economic well-being, personal security, and cultural identity. Rather than ignoring or co-opting such claims, mainstream parties must offer equally robust counternarratives.

items.title: War in an Age of Weak Powers
items.desc: The war in Iran has weakened both the United States and China, exposing the limits of their military power and strategic influence. Their troubles are creating a more dangerous geopolitical landscape while providing Europe with a rare opportunity to reform its governance model and reinvent its global role.

items.title: Hedging the AI Doomsday Risk

To guard against a danger of such extraordinary scale, governments and companies need to go beyond conventional risk-management strategies.
